newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Short Australian bonds succumb to profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Short Australian bonds succumb to profit-taking.

text.p: *The Australian bond market cooled off after Friday's heady rally as the short-end succumbed to profit-taking.
*Longer dated stock bolstered by Friday's U.S. rally.
The Australian bond market cooled off after last Friday's heady rally which followed a weak retail trade report as the short-end succumbed to profit-taking.

"The short-end had been rallying for over a week, so it's not surprising that its finally come to a halt. The offshore unloaded some stock on Friday and we've seen domestic institutions going further along the curve," one trader said.
The long-end was bolstered by a rally in U.S. Treasuries on Friday on further foreign buying, although overall local activity was more subdued, traders added.

However, analysts expect the minor setback at the short end is likely to be shortlived with three year bonds still offering a reasonable premium over the cash rate, but the resumption of the rally is likely to be on hold until after Wednesday first quarter GDP.
The market will also be keeping on the Reserve Bank at 9.30 a.m. (2330 GMT) over the next few days and when policy changes are announced with the RBA board meeting on Tuesday.
Although another easing is unlikely so soon after the May 23 rate cut, such was the surprise of the last move the market is taking nothing for granted, traders said.
"There is zero chance of a rate cut now. There is nothing really to justify another rate move, but people will still be watching their screens," one trader said.
Reuters monthly interest rate poll of economists gave a median 35 percent chance of a further easing this cycle.

"In the context of continuing evidence of subdued economic conditions, coupled with a still soft labour market, a very positive 1997 inflation outlook, and ongoing evidence of moderate broad-based wage pressures, we rate another official rate cut in the next three months as a 50/50 chance," said John Peters, senior economist at Westpac Banking Corp.

The local short end gave up ground to U.S. and Canada after last week's strong outperformance. However, the 10-year spread to Canada narrowed again ahead of today's Canadian election. New Zealand markets were closed for the Queen's Birthday holiday.
